Blood vessel walls are composed of endothelial tissue and a basal membrane lining the lumen of the vessel, concentric smooth muscle layers on top of endothelial tissue, and an adventitia over the smooth muscle layers. Relaxation of the smooth muscle layer allows the blood vessel to dilate, as it is held in a semi-constricted state by sympathetic nervous system activity. Vasodilation is the opposite of vasoconstriction, which is the narrowing of blood vessels. When blood vessels dilate, the flow of blood is increased due to a decrease in vascular resistance and increase in cardiac output*[further explanation needed*]. The primary function of vasodilation is to increase blood flow in the body to tissues that need it most.

Inflammation is the body’s natural response to injury or damage. When injury or damage occurs, specialized cells called immune cells move into the affected area to fight off the pathogen responsible for the problem. White blood cells, along with macrophages and neutrophils, are the primary cells responsible for this job.
Macrophages are the most important cells for this task. They identify the foreign particles (such as bacteria) and then either destroy them or push them into another part of the body so they can be removed. Macrophages can also become infected by the pathogen, making them part of the problem.
A macrophage is a white blood cell that has been infected by a pathogen. In this case, it becomes an “opportunistic macrophage” because instead of just fighting the pathogen, it now has the ability to spread the infection to other areas of the body. This makes the infection worse and can lead to further problems.
When inflammation occurs outside the body, it is referred to as being systemic.
Systemic inflammation is a common condition in which the body’s normal methods of fighting an infection are overwhelmed and cannot handle the job effectively. It often starts in the lymph nodes, which are small, bean-shaped clusters of immune cells located throughout the body. From there, the infection can spread to other areas of the body through the bloodstream.
The lymph nodes act as filters for the immune system, directing white blood cells to the proper location. When too many white blood cells are activated, they leak out into the bloodstream, allowing the infection to spread throughout the body.

Title: Lab Test: Reticulocyte Count
Content: + Measurement of percentage of reticulocytes in peripheral blood for evaluation of erythropoietic activity and to help direct clinical management of anemia. - The erythropoietic activity of the bone marrow and the rate of cell delivery into the peripheral circulation determine the number of reticulocytes in the peripheral blood. - Reticulocytosis (an increased number of peripheral blood reticulocytes) may be seen with anemia in the presence of functional bone marrow (e.g., blood loss, intravascular hemolysis, polycythemia vera, exogenous erythropoietin administration, or replacement of folate or iron). - In patients with sickle cell disease, the average steady-state reticulocyte count is 12% (range of 5% to 30%; normal adult range:  0.5% to 2.5% cells). + The reticulocyte count is a test for determining bone marrow function and evaluating erythropoietic activity. Because the reticulocyte count is a percentage of the total number of RBCs, a normal to low number of reticulocytes can appear high in the anemic patient, because the total number of mature RBCs is low.
